question: What is a bean definition in Spring?
title: Spring Bean Definition Explained
direct_answer: A bean definition is the metadata blueprint Spring uses to create and manage a bean. It contains the class type, scope (singleton or prototype), constructor arguments, property values, and lifecycle callbacks. Spring stores these definitions in the BeanFactory and instantiates objects from them when needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that Spring separates bean metadata (definition) from the actual object instance
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking bean definition and bean instance are the same thing, when definition is the recipe and instance is the cooked meal
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that Spring reads annotations or XML to create BeanDefinition objects before any beans are instantiated, showing you understand the two-phase process

sections.title: Bean Definition: The Blueprint for Spring Beans
sections.content: When Spring starts up, it doesn't immediately create your beans. First, it scans your code and builds **bean definitions** — metadata objects that describe HOW to create each bean. Think of it like a recipe card in a cookbook: the card tells you ingredients, cooking time, and steps, but it's not the actual dish. A bean definition stores the class name (what Java class), **scope** (singleton or prototype), constructor parameters, property values, and lifecycle hooks (init/destroy methods). Spring registers these definitions in the **BeanFactory** registry. Later, when your application needs a bean, Spring reads the definition and creates the actual instance. This separation is powerful: Spring can validate all definitions at startup, detect circular dependencies, and optimize initialization order before creating any objects. For a UserService class, the definition might say: class=UserService, scope=singleton, inject UserRepository into constructor, call an init method after construction.

sections.title: Bean Definition in Action
Key Points
content: **BeanDefinition object**: Internal Spring class holding metadata like beanClassName, scope, lazyInit, constructorArgumentValues, and propertyValues
**Registration phase**: Spring scans annotations or XML and creates BeanDefinition objects before instantiating any beans
**Scope metadata**: The definition stores whether the bean is singleton (one instance) or prototype (new instance per request)
**Dependency metadata**: Constructor args and property values are stored in the definition, not resolved until instantiation
**Lifecycle callbacks**: Init methods, destroy methods, and BeanPostProcessor hooks are part of the definition
**BeanFactory role**: Acts as the registry holding all bean definitions and uses them to create instances on demand
**Definition vs instance**: The definition is created once at startup; instances are created from it (once for singleton, many times for prototype)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A bean definition is basically the recipe Spring uses to create a bean. It's not the bean itself — it's the metadata that tells Spring how to build the bean. When Spring starts, it scans your code and creates these bean definitions first. Each definition stores things like the class type, whether it's a singleton or prototype, what dependencies to inject, and any init or destroy methods. Think of it like this: if you have a UserService class with the at-Service annotation, Spring creates a bean definition that says 'okay, this is a UserService class, it's a singleton, it needs a UserRepository injected into the constructor, and after creation call this init method.' All those definitions get stored in the BeanFactory registry. Later, when your app actually needs a UserService, Spring looks up the definition and uses it to create the instance. The key point is that Spring separates the metadata from the actual object. This lets Spring validate everything at startup, figure out the right order to create beans, and catch circular dependencies before any objects are made. A common mistake freshers make is thinking the definition and the instance are the same thing. They're not — the definition is the blueprint, the instance is what you get when Spring follows that blueprint. That's why you can have one definition but multiple instances if the bean is prototype-scoped.

beats.text: A bean definition is the metadata Spring stores to describe how to create a bean. It's not the bean itself — it's the recipe. It holds the class to instantiate, the scope (singleton or prototype), constructor arguments, properties to inject, and lifecycle method names. Spring reads all your annotations at startup and builds a registry of these definitions before creating any instances.

Separating the blueprint from the object lets Spring manage scope correctly. One definition can produce one singleton instance or hundreds of prototype instances depending on configuration. Without this separation, changing scope would require rewriting the creation logic.

items: Class: which Java class to instantiate — the core of the definition.
Scope: singleton means one shared instance; prototype means a new instance per injection.
Constructor arguments and properties: captured for dependency injection during instantiation.
Init and destroy method names: @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy hook into the lifecycle.
Lazy flag: controls whether Spring creates the bean eagerly at startup or waits until first access.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, @Service on UserService causes Spring to register a bean definition: class=UserService, scope=singleton, constructor-arg=UserRepository. Later Spring uses that definition to create one UserService instance and inject it everywhere it's needed. candidates miss: there's always exactly one bean definition per registered bean, but singleton scope means one instance while prototype scope can produce many instances from that same definition.

items: Don't confuse the definition with the instance — asking how many bean definitions exist is different from asking how many bean instances are live.
Bean definitions are frozen after context refresh — you can't add new definitions at runtime in a standard Spring Boot app.

speakable_v2.cap: The bean definition is Spring's recipe card — one recipe, but the number of dishes it produces depends on the scope.

question: What is the @Bean annotation and when do you use it?
title: @Bean Annotation in Spring — Usage and Purpose
direct_answer: The at-Bean annotation is a method-level annotation used inside a at-Configuration class to explicitly register a bean with Spring. The method's return value becomes the bean instance. You use it when you can't annotate the class itself with at-Component, typically for third-party library classes like ObjectMapper or RestTemplate.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of how to register beans when you don't control the source code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting at-Bean on a method outside a at-Configuration class, which won't work
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give real-world examples: registering Jackson's ObjectMapper, Spring's RestTemplate, or a DataSource from HikariCP

sections.title: Explicit Bean Registration with @Bean
sections.content: The **at-Bean annotation** gives you manual control over bean creation. You put it on a method inside a **at-Configuration class**, and Spring calls that method to get the bean instance. The method return type is the bean type, and the method name becomes the bean name by default. This is essential when you're working with classes from external libraries — you can't go into Jackson's source code and add at-Component to ObjectMapper, so you write a at-Bean method that creates and configures it. The annotation also lets you run custom initialization logic before returning the bean: setting properties, calling init methods, wrapping objects in proxies. Spring treats the returned object as a managed bean with full lifecycle support — dependency injection, AOP, transaction management. You have complete control: instantiate with new, call setters, choose constructor arguments, even return null if needed (though that's rare). Think of at-Bean as 'manual bean factory method' compared to at-Component which is 'automatic scan and register'.

sections.title: Registering Third-Party Beans
Key Points
content: **Method-level annotation**: at-Bean goes on a method, not a class — the method must be inside a at-Configuration class
**Return value is the bean**: Whatever the method returns becomes the Spring-managed bean instance
**Default bean name**: By default, the bean name is the method name; override with at-Bean(name="customName")
**Dependency injection in parameters**: Spring automatically injects method parameters from the context — just declare them
**Use case: third-party classes**: Essential for registering library classes you can't annotate: ObjectMapper, RestTemplate, DataSource, Executor
**Initialization control**: You can run any Java code before returning the bean — setters, builders, factory methods
**Single responsibility**: One at-Bean method should create one bean type; don't mix multiple bean creation in one method

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The at-Bean annotation is how you manually register a bean with Spring. You put it on a method inside a at-Configuration class, and whatever that method returns becomes a Spring bean. The big reason you'd use it is when you're working with a class from a library — like Jackson's ObjectMapper or Spring's RestTemplate — and you can't go add at-Component to that class because you don't own the source code. So you write a at-Bean method that creates the instance, configures it however you need, and returns it. Spring then manages that object as a bean. For example, if you need an ObjectMapper bean, you'd write a method like 'public ObjectMapper objectMapper', annotate it with at-Bean, create the ObjectMapper inside the method, maybe register some modules or set serialization options, and return it. The method name becomes the bean name by default — 'objectMapper' in this case. You can also have Spring inject dependencies into the method parameters. If your bean needs a UserRepository, just add it as a parameter and Spring will pass it in. One thing freshers miss: at-Bean only works inside a at-Configuration class. If you put it on a random class method, Spring won't see it. Common examples where you'd use at-Bean are ObjectMapper for JSON, RestTemplate for HTTP calls, DataSource for database connections, and ThreadPoolExecutor for async tasks.

beats.text: @Bean is a method-level annotation placed inside a @Configuration class. The method creates and returns the object you want Spring to manage. Spring registers the return value as a bean, using the method name as the default bean name. The method can accept parameters — Spring resolves and injects them from the context automatically.

@Component works only when you own the source code and can add annotations. But third-party classes like Jackson's ObjectMapper or a database connection pool don't have @Component on them. @Bean lets you write the creation code yourself and hand the result to Spring.

items: Basic: @Bean on a no-arg method — Spring calls it once and registers the return value.
Named: @Bean(name="myBean") overrides the default method-name-based name.
With parameters: Spring injects each parameter from the context before calling the method.
Combined with @Scope, @Primary, @Lazy, or @DependsOn for advanced lifecycle control.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, AppConfig is a @Configuration class with an objectMapper() method annotated @Bean. Inside, you call new ObjectMapper() and register the JavaTimeModule so Java 8 date types serialize correctly. Spring calls this method once and makes the configured ObjectMapper available for injection anywhere in the app. sharp edge: if you put @Bean in a class annotated only with @Component (not @Configuration), the CGLIB proxy is absent and calling one @Bean method from another will create a new instance each time — breaking singleton semantics.

items: @Bean must live in a class that Spring scans — if the @Configuration class is outside the component scan package, its beans won't be registered.
Avoid business logic inside @Bean methods — keep them as thin factory methods.

speakable_v2.cap: @Bean is your escape hatch for beans you can't annotate directly — use it in @Configuration to register any class as a Spring-managed bean.

question: What is @Configuration in Spring and how is it different from @Component?
title: @Configuration vs @Component in Spring
direct_answer: at-Configuration marks a class as a bean definition source containing at-Bean methods. Spring CGLIB-proxies the class so calling a at-Bean method from another method returns the singleton instance, not a new object. at-Component just registers the class itself as a bean. at-Configuration is a specialized at-Component.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the CGLIB proxy behavior that enforces singleton semantics for at-Bean methods
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that at-Configuration creates a proxy to intercept at-Bean method calls and return the same singleton
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain what happens if you call a at-Bean method directly from another at-Bean method in a at-Configuration class versus a plain at-Component class

sections.title: Understanding @Configuration and Its Proxy Behavior
sections.content: Both **at-Configuration** and **at-Component** register a class as a Spring bean, but at-Configuration has special behavior for at-Bean methods. When you annotate a class with at-Configuration, Spring doesn't use your class directly — it creates a **CGLIB proxy subclass** that intercepts method calls. WHY? To enforce singleton semantics for at-Bean methods. If you have two at-Bean methods where one calls the other, without the proxy you'd get two different instances. The proxy intercepts the call and returns the singleton from the Spring container instead. This is critical for dependency consistency. With plain at-Component, Spring doesn't create this proxy, so if you call a at-Bean method from another method in the same class, you'll invoke the method directly and get a new object each time. at-Configuration is actually a meta-annotation that includes at-Component, so it does everything at-Component does PLUS adds the proxy layer. In practice, you use at-Configuration for classes that define at-Bean methods (configuration classes) and at-Component for classes that ARE the bean (service classes, repositories).

rows: Register the class as a bean

sections.title: When to Use Each
sections.content: Use **at-Configuration** when your class is a configuration source that defines at-Bean methods. If you have at-Bean method A that calls at-Bean method B, the proxy ensures both beans get the same instance of B from the container. This is the standard pattern for application configuration classes: AppConfig, DatabaseConfig, SecurityConfig. Use **at-Component** (or its specializations at-Service, at-Repository, at-Controller) when the class itself is the bean you want Spring to manage. For example, UserService is annotated with at-Service because UserService is the bean — you're not defining other beans inside it. If you mistakenly use at-Component on a class with at-Bean methods, inter-bean method calls won't go through the container, breaking singleton guarantees. The rule of thumb: configuration classes that produce beans get at-Configuration; service classes that are beans get at-Component or its specializations.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **CGLIB proxy**: at-Configuration triggers CGLIB proxy creation — Spring subclasses your config class at runtime to intercept method calls
**Singleton enforcement**: When one at-Bean method calls another in a at-Configuration class, the proxy intercepts and returns the container's singleton
**at-Component inheritance**: at-Configuration is meta-annotated with at-Component, so it's component-scanned and registered as a bean
**Direct method calls**: In a plain at-Component class, calling a at-Bean method directly bypasses the container and creates a new instance
**Full vs Lite mode**: at-Configuration is 'Full' mode (proxied); at-Component with at-Bean methods is 'Lite' mode (no proxy)
**Use case separation**: Use at-Configuration for classes that define beans; use at-Component for classes that are beans
**Performance cost**: CGLIB proxies add slight overhead, but it's negligible compared to the correctness guarantee

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: at-Configuration and at-Component both register a class as a Spring bean, but they're used for different purposes and at-Configuration has special proxy behavior. You use at-Configuration on classes that define at-Bean methods — basically configuration classes. You use at-Component on classes that are themselves the bean, like service classes or repositories. The big difference is that Spring creates a CGLIB proxy for at-Configuration classes. Here's why that matters. Let's say you have two at-Bean methods in a at-Configuration class, and one calls the other. Without the proxy, you'd get a new instance every time you call that method. But with the proxy, Spring intercepts the call and returns the singleton instance from the container instead. This keeps your beans consistent. If you used plain at-Component on a configuration class, that inter-bean method call would just invoke the Java method directly, creating a new object and breaking the singleton contract. at-Configuration is actually a specialized version of at-Component — it's meta-annotated with at-Component, so it gets picked up by component scanning. The rule is simple: if your class has at-Bean methods that define other beans, use at-Configuration. If your class is the bean itself, use at-Component or one of its specializations like at-Service or at-Repository. A common mistake is using at-Component for configuration classes and wondering why you're getting multiple instances of your beans.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Both get picked up by component scanning, but @Configuration gets a superpower: a proxy that guarantees singleton semantics for every @Bean method.

groups.heading: @Configuration
groups.text: Marks a class as a factory for @Bean definitions. Spring wraps it in a CGLIB proxy at startup. When any @Bean method is called — even directly from another @Bean method — the proxy intercepts and returns the existing singleton instead of creating a new object.

groups.heading: @Component
groups.text: Registers the class itself as a bean. No CGLIB proxy. If you put @Bean methods inside a @Component class, calling one @Bean method directly from another will bypass Spring and create a brand new object each time — breaking singletons.

items: Use @Configuration whenever you define @Bean methods — the proxy guarantee is essential for correct singleton behavior.
Use @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods=false) when your @Bean methods are standalone and never call each other — it's faster to start up.
Use @Component for classes that don't define beans, like services, listeners, and utilities.

beats.text: gotcha: in our Spring Boot 3.2 AppConfig, beanA() calls beanC() directly. With @Configuration, Spring's proxy intercepts that call and returns the same C singleton that beanB() already received. Without the proxy (if you used @Component), A and B would each get a different C instance — subtle bugs with shared state.

speakable_v2.cap: @Configuration is @Component plus a proxy. Use @Configuration for bean factories; use @Component for everything else.

question: What is @Lazy in Spring and when would you use it?
title: @Lazy Bean Initialization in Spring
direct_answer: at-Lazy defers bean creation until the bean is first accessed. By default, singleton beans are created eagerly at application startup. Marking a bean or injection point with at-Lazy delays instantiation until it's actually needed. Useful for expensive beans or breaking circular dependencies, but delays error detection until runtime.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Spring's eager versus lazy initialization strategies
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Overusing at-Lazy to speed up startup without understanding it hides errors that eager initialization would catch
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the trade-off: at-Lazy improves startup time but moves initialization errors from startup to runtime when the bean is first used

sections.title: Lazy Initialization in Spring
sections.content: By default, Spring creates all **singleton beans** at application startup — this is **eager initialization**. It validates dependencies, detects circular references, and surfaces configuration errors immediately. But some beans are expensive to create: they might open database connections, load large datasets, or initialize third-party libraries. If you don't need them right away, creating them at startup wastes time and memory. **at-Lazy** tells Spring to skip creation until the bean is first accessed. You can put at-Lazy on the bean definition itself (the class or at-Bean method) or on an injection point (constructor parameter, field). When on the bean, Spring creates a proxy that defers instantiation. When on an injection point, Spring injects a lazy proxy that triggers creation on first method call. The trade-off is startup speed versus fail-fast behavior. Lazy beans can have configuration errors that won't surface until minutes or hours after startup when someone actually uses that feature. For freshers, eager initialization is safer — you want to know about problems immediately, not when a user triggers a rare code path.

sections.title: Trade-offs of Lazy Initialization
sections.content: **Pros: Faster startup time** — If you have many beans or some are expensive to initialize (large file parsing, network calls, heavy computation), deferring creation can shave seconds off startup. This matters for development cycles (faster restart) and serverless deployments (cold start time). **Pros: Lower memory footprint at startup** — Beans that allocate significant memory (caches, connection pools) won't consume resources until actually needed. If a feature is rarely used, you might never create the bean. **Cons: Delayed error detection** — Misconfigurations, missing dependencies, or init method exceptions won't appear until runtime. A production bug could hide for weeks until a user triggers the lazy path. Eager init acts as a startup smoke test. **Cons: Unpredictable first-use latency** — The first request that needs a lazy bean will pause while Spring creates it. If initialization takes 5 seconds, that user gets a 5-second delay. With eager init, everyone shares the startup cost. **Cons: Harder debugging** — Stack traces from lazy init errors happen deep in request handling, not during clear startup phases. Troubleshooting is harder. **When to use: circular dependencies** — at-Lazy can break circular references by deferring one side of the cycle. **When to use: expensive optional features** — Reporting modules, admin dashboards, batch jobs that run daily but not every request.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Eager by default**: Spring singleton beans are created at startup unless marked at-Lazy; this fail-fast approach catches errors early
**Lazy proxy**: at-Lazy on a bean creates a proxy object; the real bean is instantiated on first method call
**Injection point lazy**: at-Lazy on a constructor parameter or at-Autowired field injects a lazy proxy regardless of the bean's own laziness
**Circular dependency workaround**: Marking one side of a circular dependency with at-Lazy can break the cycle by deferring initialization
**Prototype beans**: Prototype-scoped beans are always lazy — they're created on each request, not at startup
**Global lazy init**: You can set spring.main.lazy-initialization=true to make all beans lazy, but this is risky for production
**Not a performance fix**: Don't use at-Lazy to hide slow startup — fix the root cause of expensive initialization instead

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: at-Lazy tells Spring to delay creating a bean until it's actually needed, instead of creating it at startup. By default, Spring creates all singleton beans when the application starts — that's called eager initialization. It's safer because any configuration problems show up immediately. But if you have a bean that's expensive to create, like one that loads a huge dataset or opens a database connection pool, and you don't need it right away, you can mark it with at-Lazy. Then Spring will skip it during startup and only create it the first time someone actually uses it. You can put at-Lazy on the bean class itself, on a at-Bean method, or on an injection point like a constructor parameter. When you do that, Spring injects a proxy object, and the real bean gets created on the first method call. Here's the trade-off: lazy initialization speeds up startup and saves memory, but it also delays errors. If your lazy bean has a configuration problem, you won't know until runtime when a user triggers that code path. That could be hours or days later. For freshers, I'd say stick with eager initialization unless you have a specific reason to defer. Eager init is like running tests at compile time — you catch problems early. There's one common use case for at-Lazy though: breaking circular dependencies. If bean A needs bean B and bean B needs bean A, you can mark one injection as at-Lazy to break the cycle.

Don't use it broadly in production. production trap: @Lazy on a misconfigured bean means the error doesn't appear until that bean is first requested — possibly hours into a production run.

items: You're adding @Lazy to fix a startup performance problem — profile first to confirm the bean is actually the bottleneck.
You're using @Lazy to work around a circular dependency — that's a workaround, not a fix. Refactor the design instead.

question: What is @DependsOn in Spring and when do you need it?
title: @DependsOn Bean Ordering in Spring
direct_answer: at-DependsOn forces Spring to initialize specified beans before creating the annotated bean. It controls initialization order when there's no direct dependency that Spring can detect. Use it when one bean has a side effect — like schema creation or static resource setup — that another bean relies on, but there's no at-Autowired field linking them.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of explicit bean initialization ordering when implicit dependency wiring isn't enough
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using at-DependsOn when a proper at-Autowired dependency would handle ordering automatically and more clearly
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that at-DependsOn is for initialization order, not runtime dependencies — the beans don't reference each other, but one must start first

sections.title: Controlling Bean Initialization Order with @DependsOn
sections.content: Spring normally handles bean initialization order automatically based on **dependency relationships** — if ServiceA autowires RepositoryB, Spring creates RepositoryB first. But sometimes beans have hidden dependencies that Spring can't see. Bean A might rely on a side effect of Bean B's initialization: B sets up a database schema, registers a shutdown hook, or populates a static cache. There's no at-Autowired field linking them, so Spring doesn't know about the relationship. **at-DependsOn** solves this by explicitly declaring initialization order. You annotate Bean A with at-DependsOn("beanB") and Spring guarantees beanB is fully initialized before creating Bean A. The beans don't reference each other in code — at-DependsOn is purely about timing. Common use case: a SchemaInitializer bean that creates database tables must run before a RepositoryBean that queries those tables, even though the repository doesn't inject the initializer. Another example: a CacheWarmer bean that pre-loads data must finish before a ServiceBean that reads from the cache. Important distinction: at-DependsOn affects initialization order, not destruction order (though Spring does destroy dependents first).

sections.title: Using @DependsOn for Initialization Ordering
Key Points
content: **Initialization ordering**: at-DependsOn ensures named beans are fully initialized before the annotated bean is created
**No runtime dependency**: The beans don't reference each other in code — this is about startup sequence, not object references
**Side-effect dependencies**: Use when one bean's initialization has a side effect (schema creation, static setup) that another bean relies on
**Bean name reference**: at-DependsOn takes bean names as strings, not class types; names must match exactly
**Multiple dependencies**: You can specify multiple beans: at-DependsOn({"beanA", "beanB", "beanC"})
**Avoid overuse**: If you can express the relationship with at-Autowired, do that — it's clearer and type-safe; at-DependsOn is a last resort
**Circular with DependsOn**: If Bean A depends on Bean B and Bean B depends on Bean A, Spring throws a circular dependency error at startup

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: at-DependsOn is how you tell Spring to initialize one bean before another when there's no direct dependency between them. Normally, if ServiceA has an at-Autowired field for RepositoryB, Spring knows to create RepositoryB first. But sometimes beans have hidden relationships. Maybe you have a DatabaseSchemaInitializer bean that runs SQL scripts to create tables during its constructor. Then you have a OrderRepository bean that queries those tables. The repository doesn't inject the initializer — it just needs the tables to exist. Spring doesn't know about this relationship, so it might try to create the repository first, and you'd get an error because the tables don't exist yet. That's where at-DependsOn comes in. You'd put at-DependsOn with the initializer's bean name on the repository, and Spring will guarantee the initializer runs first. The key thing to understand is that at-DependsOn is about initialization order, not runtime dependencies. The beans don't reference each other in code. Another example is a CacheWarmer bean that pre-loads data into a cache during startup. Any service that reads from that cache should use at-DependsOn to make sure the cache is warmed up first. A common mistake is using at-DependsOn when you could just inject the dependency normally. If Bean A actually uses Bean B at runtime, just autowire it — Spring will handle the order automatically and your code is clearer. Only use at-DependsOn when the dependency is a side effect, not a real object reference.

speakable_v2.hook: @DependsOn is for the invisible dependency — when bean B needs bean A to have already run, but doesn't inject A directly.

beats.text: @DependsOn tells Spring to initialize a named bean before the annotated bean, even though there's no direct @Autowired link between them. It's purely an ordering guarantee. Spring normally determines initialization order from its dependency graph — @DependsOn extends that graph with an explicit edge for cases Spring can't infer automatically.

Spring can only detect order dependencies it can see — @Autowired fields and constructor parameters. Implicit side-effect dependencies, like 'bean A must run DDL before bean B reads the tables,' are invisible to Spring. @DependsOn makes them explicit.

items: Single dependency: @DependsOn("beanName") — ensures one named bean initializes first.
Multiple dependencies: @DependsOn({"beanA", "beanB"}) — both must initialize before the annotated bean.
Applicable to @Bean methods and @Component classes alike.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, DatabaseSchemaInitializer runs Flyway migrations at startup. CacheLoader reads from the freshly-migrated tables. CacheLoader doesn't inject DatabaseSchemaInitializer — it just needs the tables to exist. You add @DependsOn("databaseSchemaInitializer") on CacheLoader's @Bean method so Spring guarantees the migration completes first. non-obvious: if CacheLoader did @Autowire DatabaseSchemaInitializer, Spring would already order them correctly — @DependsOn is only needed when the link is invisible.

items: Don't use @DependsOn when a direct @Autowired dependency would do the job — the explicit injection is both cleaner and self-documenting.
Frequent use of @DependsOn is a design smell — it often means initialization logic should be consolidated into one bean.

speakable_v2.cap: @DependsOn is a last resort for side-effect ordering — if you can model the dependency explicitly with @Autowired, do that instead.

question: What is bean naming in Spring and how do you set a custom bean name?
title: Spring Bean Naming Conventions
direct_answer: Spring beans are named to enable lookup and distinguish multiple beans of the same type. By default, at-Component beans are named after the class with a lowercase first letter. at-Bean methods use the method name. Set custom names with at-Component value, at-Bean name attribute, or at-Qualifier on the bean definition.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of Spring's bean naming conventions and why names matter
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the default lowercase-first-letter convention or that you can have multiple beans of the same type distinguished by name
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain when you'd need custom names: when you have multiple beans of the same type and use at-Qualifier to select which one to inject

sections.title: Bean Naming in Spring
sections.content: Every Spring bean has a **name** — a unique identifier in the application context. Names are used for lookup (applicationContext.getBean("beanName")), logging, debugging, and most importantly, for **disambiguation when multiple beans of the same type exist**. Spring generates default names automatically: for a class annotated with at-Component, at-Service, or at-Repository, the default name is the class name with the first letter lowercase: UserService becomes "userService", OrderRepository becomes "orderRepository". For at-Bean methods in a at-Configuration class, the method name is the default bean name: a method named objectMapper creates a bean named "objectMapper". You can override defaults by providing a value in the annotation: at-Component("myCustomName") or at-Bean(name="myBean"). Bean names must be unique within the application context — if you register two beans with the same name, the second overwrites the first (or Spring throws an error in strict mode). Custom names are essential when you have multiple beans of the same type: maybe two DataSource beans for different databases. You'd name them "primaryDataSource" and "secondaryDataSource", then use at-Qualifier("primaryDataSource") to specify which one to inject.

sections.title: Bean Naming Examples
Key Points
content: **Default naming for components**: Class name with lowercase first letter — UserService becomes "userService"
**Default naming for @Bean**: Method name becomes the bean name — public DataSource mainDb() creates bean "mainDb"
**Custom names**: Override with @Component("customName"), @Bean(name="customName"), or @Qualifier("customName") on the definition
**Uniqueness**: Bean names must be unique in the context; duplicate names cause overwrites or errors depending on configuration
**Multiple beans of same type**: Use distinct names and @Qualifier to disambiguate when injecting
**Lookup by name**: applicationContext.getBean("beanName") retrieves a bean by its name at runtime
**Alias support**: You can define multiple names for one bean with @Bean(name={"name1","alias1","alias2"})

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Every Spring bean has a name that identifies it in the application context. By default, Spring generates the name automatically. If you have a class like UserService annotated with at-Service, the default bean name is 'userService' — the class name with the first letter lowercase. For at-Bean methods in a configuration class, the method name becomes the bean name. So if you have a method 'public DataSource dataSource', the bean is named 'dataSource'. You can customize the name by passing a value to the annotation. For example, at-Service with a value like 'myUserService' or at-Bean with name equals 'customDataSource'. Why does this matter? Bean names are mainly used when you have multiple beans of the same type. Let's say you have two DataSource beans — one for your main database and one for a reporting database. You'd give them different names like 'primaryDataSource' and 'reportingDataSource'. Then when you inject a DataSource into a service, you'd use the at-Qualifier annotation with the name to tell Spring which one you want. Without that, Spring wouldn't know which DataSource to inject and you'd get an error. Another use for names is when you need to look up a bean at runtime using applicationContext.getBean with the name. A common mistake freshers make is not knowing the lowercase-first-letter convention, or not realizing you can have multiple beans of the same type as long as they have different names. The key is that bean names let you distinguish between beans when types alone aren't enough.

seo.metaTitle: Spring Bean Naming Conventions | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Learn Spring bean naming conventions, how default names are derived from class names, and how to set custom names with @Component and @Bean annotations.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 app with @Service, @Repository, and constructor injection
speakable_v2.hook: Spring names your beans for free — but when you have two beans of the same type, knowing those names is the only way to pick the right one.

beats.text: Every Spring bean has a name — a string identifier used to look it up and to match @Qualifier references. By default, @Component and its specializations derive the name from the class name with the first letter lowercased. @Bean methods use the method name. Custom names override the default by passing a string value to the annotation.

Bean names are how you resolve ambiguity. When you have two beans of the same type, type-based injection alone fails. @Qualifier uses the bean name to select the right one. Understanding names is also essential when using applicationContext.getBean() for dynamic lookup.

items: Default for @Service/@Component: class name with lowercase first letter — UserService becomes userService.
Default for @Bean method: method name — public DataSource primaryDataSource() becomes bean name primaryDataSource.
Custom single name: @Component("myBean") or @Bean(name="myBean").
Multiple aliases: @Bean(name={"primaryDs", "mainDs"}) — the bean answers to either name.

beats.text: In our Spring Boot 3.2 app, there are two DataSource beans: devDataSource() and prodDataSource(). Their names are devDataSource and prodDataSource by default. You inject the right one with @Qualifier("devDataSource") at the injection point. gotcha: if you rename the method from devDataSource to devDs, the default name changes too — and any @Qualifier("devDataSource") references break silently. Use explicit @Bean(name="devDataSource") to lock the name.

items: Renaming a method that provides a @Bean changes the default bean name — existing @Qualifier references will break.
Two beans can't share the same name in the same context — Spring throws BeanDefinitionOverrideException unless you explicitly allow overriding.

speakable_v2.cap: Know the default naming rule, name your beans explicitly when they'll be referenced by @Qualifier, and never let a method rename silently change a bean name you depend on.
